about.dates: This report covers your session on Wednesday 9 September 2026 and was prepared on 9 September 2026. If a session is re-analysed, the report is prepared again and carries the new date.
about.footnote: Measured and prepared with PinPoint Studio. Swing images show only the golfer; video stays in the studio.
about.measured: 7 swings with a 6 iron, filmed face-on at high frame rate. Your body positions are read from the video by pose tracking.
about.notChecked: Some things could not be checked on every swing. When your hips turned fastest: the face-on camera cannot time a turn while you are square to it; a down-the-line camera or a body sensor can (7 of 7 swings). How fast the club was moving at its peak: our cameras could see it, but not well enough to judge (7 of 7 swings). Hip turn at the top: a single face-on camera cannot measure how far you turn; a down-the-line camera or a body sensor can (7 of 7 swings). Chest turn at the finish: a single face-on camera cannot measure how far you turn; a down-the-line camera or a body sensor can (7 of 7 swings). One more is listed in the technical appendix. Nothing in this report depends on them.
about.ranges: Each habit is judged against a target range. Most ranges are coaching judgement, set from what good ball-strikers do; a few come from published measurements. They are not fitted to you. A swing outside the range is not a mistake in itself — it is where the evidence points. “Ruled out” on a work-on page means measured, and fine, on these swings with these cameras — not gone for good.

rules.body: When one habit sets up another, working on the first often fixes the second for free. We only put one behind another when your swings show it: the second goes away on the swings where the first does.

workOns.check: Film face-on. At impact your chest should be roughly square to the ball and still turning, with your hips already a little more open than your chest.
workOns.coachTerm: Coaches call the habit Chest peaks after impact.
workOns.cue: Feel your chest turn hard toward the ball as you come down, rather than saving the turn for after it.

drills.instruction: Make swings with a one-second pause at the top. From the pause, start down with your lower body, letting your weight move toward your lead foot while your chest stays behind the ball for a moment. Start with half swings and short irons.
drills.label: Pause at the top
drills.note: The pause is a rehearsal, not a new swing. Once the order feels natural, let the pause shrink until it has gone.
drills.targets: To give your lower body time to start the downswing, so your upper body is not rushed toward the ball.

workOns.goal: Let your chest reach full speed before the ball
workOns.kicker: Work-on 1 of 5  ·  P7, at impact  ·  7 of 7 swings
workOns.name: Chest peaks after impact
workOns.saw: Your chest is still speeding up after the ball — on all 7 swings, no change from first swing to last. Typical when your chest reached full speed: 18 ms after impact.
workOns.why: A chest still speeding up after the ball has not passed its speed on to your arms and the club in time for the strike.

workOns.check: Film face-on. At the top your head and chest should sit a little behind the ball, never toward the target.
workOns.coachTerm: Coaches call the habit Reverse spine angle at P4, or “leaning left at the top”, “forward spine angle at the top”.
workOns.cue: At the top, feel your breastbone stay over your trail thigh.

drills.equipment: a mirror, or a phone on a stand
drills.instruction: Without a ball, hold a club across your chest. Turn to the top and check in a mirror, or on a phone face-on, that your head and chest sit a little behind the ball, with your upper body tilted slightly away from the target. Make ten slow turns.
drills.label: Club across the chest
drills.note: A short turn often hides inside this one: if the shoulders cannot turn further, the body tips instead, and a physical check of your upper back comes first.
drills.targets: To feel your upper body staying behind the ball as it turns, rather than tipping toward the target or hanging too far back.

workOns.goal: Lean slightly away from the target at the top
workOns.kicker: Work-on 2 of 5  ·  P4, at the top  ·  5 of 7 swings
workOns.name: Reverse spine angle at P4
workOns.saw: You lean toward the target at the top — on 5 of 7 swings, no change from first swing to last. Typical lean away from the target at the top: 5° the other way (you lean more toward the target at the top), against a target of 0° or more; this is mostly a small miss, but well past the range on 2 of 7 swings.
workOns.target: Lean away from the target at the top: 0° or more, on most swings. Today: 5° the other way (you lean more toward the target at the top).
workOns.why: Leaning toward the target at the top strains your lower back and makes it hard to start down smoothly.

workOns.check: Film face-on with a stick standing upright just outside your trail hip at address. At the top your hip should turn without pushing past it.
workOns.coachTerm: Coaches call the habit Sway, or “swaying off the ball”, “lateral slide back”.
workOns.cue: Feel your trail hip pocket turn behind you, as if your trail leg were a post you turn around.

drills.equipment: an alignment stick outside the trail hip, optional
drills.instruction: Take your address position, make a slow backswing turn, and stop at the top. Feel the pressure in the trail hip socket rather than on the outside of the trail foot. Hold for three seconds, then return.
drills.label: Trail hip load and hold
drills.note: The stick is a feedback aid, not the drill. If the hip cannot rotate internally, the slide is the body finding the only route it has.
drills.targets: To feel the trail hip accepting the turn instead of the pelvis sliding away from the target.

drills.instruction: Set up with your trail heel a few inches from a wall and make backswings without touching it.
drills.label: Trail heel against a wall
drills.note: Pairs with the hip load drill; this one gives the feedback, that one gives the feel.
drills.targets: To feel a backswing that turns rather than slides.

Typical hip movement away from the target going back, minus meaning toward it: 23% stance width, against a target of 20% stance width or less; this is a small miss: just outside the range, never far.

workOns.target: Hip movement away from the target going back, minus meaning toward it: 20% stance width or less, on most swings. Today: 23% stance width.
workOns.why: When your hips slide away, the bottom of your swing moves and contact gets harder to repeat.

workOns.check: Film face-on. At the top your lead knee should still sit roughly over your lead foot, rather than pointing in at the ball.
workOns.coachTerm: Coaches call the habit Lead knee works in at the top, or “lead knee kicks in”, “left knee falls in”.
workOns.cue: Feel your lead knee stay over your lead foot while your trail hip turns behind you.

drills.equipment: an alignment stick outside the trail hip, optional
drills.instruction: Take your address position, make a slow backswing turn, and stop at the top. Feel the pressure in the trail hip socket rather than on the outside of the trail foot. Hold for three seconds, then return.
drills.label: Trail hip load and hold
drills.note: The stick is a feedback aid, not the drill. If the hip cannot rotate internally, the slide is the body finding the only route it has.
drills.targets: To feel the trail hip accepting the turn instead of the pelvis sliding away from the target.

drills.instruction: Make three-quarter backswings keeping your lead heel planted, turning only as far as you comfortably can. Then hit a few shots, letting the heel come up only as much as it needs to.
drills.label: Lead heel planted turns
drills.note: Many good players lift the lead heel, and a small lift is fine. If your turn becomes very short with the heel down, the lift is giving you turn your hips or upper back cannot, so check those before cutting it out.
drills.targets: To find out how much turn you have without the heel, and to keep any heel lift small and repeatable.

workOns.figureLabel: Each dot is one swing: how far your lead knee works in at the top, in percent of stance width.
workOns.goal: Let your lead knee hold its place going back
workOns.kicker: Work-on 4 of 5  ·  P4, at the top  ·  7 of 7 swings
workOns.name: Lead knee works in at the top
workOns.saw: Your lead knee works in going back — on all 7 swings, no change from first swing to last. Typical how far your lead knee works in at the top: 18% stance width, against a target of 16% stance width or less; this is mostly a small miss, but well past the range on 1 of 7 swings.
workOns.target: How far your lead knee works in at the top: 16% stance width or less, on most swings. Today: 18% stance width.
workOns.why: Your lead knee working in feels like a turn without being one, so there is less to unwind and less speed.

workOns.check: Film face-on. Halfway down, your hands should still be in front of the middle of your chest, with your chest already turning toward the ball.
workOns.coachTerm: Coaches call the habit Arms outrun the chest, or “arms first”, “arms take over”.
workOns.cue: Feel your arms and the club stay in front of your chest as it turns, as if your chest were carrying them down.

drills.instruction: Tuck a small towel under your lead upper arm and make three-quarter swings without dropping it.
drills.label: Towel under the lead arm
drills.note: Easy to overdo. The arm should stay connected, not pinned — a swing with no separation at all is its own fault.
drills.targets: To feel the lead arm and the chest moving as one unit through the backswing.

drills.instruction: Make swings with a one-second pause at the top. From the pause, start down with your lower body, letting your weight move toward your lead foot while your chest stays behind the ball for a moment. Start with half swings and short irons.
drills.label: Pause at the top
drills.note: The pause is a rehearsal, not a new swing. Once the order feels natural, let the pause shrink until it has gone.
drills.targets: To give your lower body time to start the downswing, so your upper body is not rushed toward the ball.

workOns.goal: Turn your chest and let your arms follow
workOns.kicker: Work-on 5 of 5  ·  P7, at impact  ·  7 of 7 swings
workOns.name: Arms outrun the chest
workOns.saw: Your arms race ahead of your chest coming down — on all 7 swings, no change from first swing to last. Typical when your chest reached full speed: 18 ms after impact.
workOns.why: When your arms take over before your chest has turned, the speed your body made is left behind and your arms have to make it alone.
